summary: Instagram is where almost all the audience is: most Hindi videos get 500-1,400 views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 60 views. The best performers are short, surprising 'robot/sensor does not see or hear what you think' videos, especially clap switch, line follower, gyro and IR robot topics. Newer videos (mid-to-late November) on niche topics like soil, TDS, thermocouple and breathalyzer are getting much less reach, and the English video and the early YouTube-only posts did poorly.
winningPattern: Robot or maker-project subjects (clap switch, line follower, gyro balancing robot, IR obstacle avoidance) with a myth-busting hook in Hinglish such as 'X doesn't do what you think, it only does Y', plus an emoji and #shorts. Posted on Instagram first, where it gets 1,000+ views; YouTube only gets a meaningful audience (400-680 views) when the topic is a classic robot/sensor that people search for, such as clap switch or PIR. Saves come from 'how a robot works' topics and shares come from surprising everyday-life facts (sunburn in clouds, soil sensor), so both formats have a role.
doMore: Make more robot and Arduino project explainers (balancing robot, line follower, obstacle avoider, clap switch) since they get the most views and saves
Keep the 'it doesn't see/hear X, it only senses Y' hook, which fits the top videos
Post every video to Instagram as well as YouTube; 11 videos had zero Instagram views
Make surprising everyday-life explainers with a clear 'wait, really?' fact for shares, like the UV sensor and soil sensor videos
Add a closing line asking viewers to save the video for their next project, to lift saves
stopDoing: Niche single-component topics with no robot or visible action (TDS meter, thermocouple, breathalyzer, KY-038)
Generic 'How does X work? 🤔' titles and English-only uploads, which got the weakest results
Posting several near-duplicate videos on the same sensor within days (clap switch, IR heat sensor)
